---
title: "Hydra extensions"
---

The branch 'hydra_extensions' adds ports of Hydra-NL routines to pydra_core: percentiles, illustration points and the
breakdown of the frequency per water system, plus compiled loops and caches that speed up the calculations. This page
holds the background of these modules: the Hydra-NL routines they follow and the choices made in the port. The
docstrings in the code only describe what a module, class or function does.

## Scenarios

'calculation_settings.sqlite' holds a full set of settings per scenario: 'BOI2023_2035' (the default),
'BOI2023_2075_Mn', 'BOI2023_2125_Mn' and 'WBI2017'. The choice is the argument 'scenario' of 'HRDatabase.get_settings' and
'HRDatabase.create_location'; an unknown name is an error. The statistics are in 'data/statistics/WBI2017' and
'data/statistics/BOI2023', the paths in the settings carry the folder name, and the files keep their name from
Hydra-NL. Per scenario the database also holds the sea level points of the coast, the Wadden Sea and the Western
Scheldt, the closing function of the Europoort barrier ('europoort_barrier_closing_function'; a closing function in
the HRD comes first) and the prediction error of the Europoort barrier per zone of 'lower_river_settings.shp'
('EuropoortBarrierZones').

The BOI2023 scenarios are made by 'tools/import_hydranl_statistics.py' from an installation of Hydra-NL; its docstring
says where each value comes from. What it reports for Hydra-NL 2.9.2:

* The Meuse tidal is measured at Borgharen (river 4) instead of Lith (river 3).
* Hydra-NL 2.9.2 has no discharge statistics of Olst for 2075 and 2125 (a dummy file), so the IJssel delta has no
  'discharge_probability' in those scenarios.
* 'm_step' of the sea stays 0.01 as in WBI2017: Hydra-NL has 0.1 in both versions, the coarser grid is a choice of the
  caller per quantity.
* The Hollandsche IJssel has no river index in pydra_core; its discharge numbers are looked up with river 2 (Rhine)
  of Hydra-NL.

## core/memory.py

Memory of calculations within one Python process, so that a second question on the same location is fast.

There are two stores, both only in the memory of the process; a new process starts empty:

- 'crest_level_tables' keeps the crest level tables of 'CrestLevelTables.crest_level_table' (at most 50,000).
  The ports in 'hydra/' use it when the caller passes no crest level function of its own.
- 'calculations' keeps the calculation objects of the ports in 'hydra/' and the crest level line of the Rhine-Meuse
  delta (at most 16). Calling a constructor again with the same arguments returns the kept object.

The label of everything kept holds all settings of the location, the time the database was last changed and all
other arguments; the label of a crest level table also holds a fingerprint of the loading grid. A changed setting,
an edited database or another grid therefore gives a new calculation. When a store is full, the entry used longest
ago falls out.

The percentiles of the IJssel-Vecht delta and the percentiles and crest level line of the Rhine-Meuse delta calculate
their crest level tables ahead in worker processes ('Memory.calculate_ahead') and keep them in 'crest_level_tables'; only
from 'MIN_POINTS_PARALLEL' points together, which in practice means with model uncertainty.

```python
from pydra_core.core import memory

memory.crest_level_tables.max_size = 10_000
memory.calculations.enabled = False
memory.processes = 1  # no worker processes
memory.Memory.clear()
```

A kept object or table is shared by everyone who asks for it: a kept table is read-only, and the ports only add to
their own caches after they are built, so the results do not depend on what was asked before.

## hydra

Ports of Hydra-NL routines.

'library' holds the routines that are shared by all water systems: grids and densities, interpolation, contours
(ISOLIJN), wave processing (VERWERKGOLF), percentiles and the scaling of the breakdown (SCHAALUITSPLITS). The
'compiled_*' modules hold compiled loops for the illustration point scans of a 3D loading field with a barrier, the
block probability over wind segments and the masked breakdown of the Rhine-Meuse delta.

'percentiles' and 'illustration_points' are the Hydra-NL percentiles and illustration point of the lakes and the upper
rivers.

'illustration_points_3d' is the illustration point on a 3D loading field with a storm surge barrier, shared by the
fresh water systems with a barrier; 'ijssel_vecht_delta' fills it in for the IJssel-Vecht delta and the Ramspol
barrier.

The ports keep their calculation objects and crest level tables in 'core.memory', within the Python process: building
a port again with the same arguments returns the kept object. 'core.memory' tells how to switch this off and how to
set the maximum sizes.

## hydra/library.py

The ported Hydra-NL routines that do not depend on a water system.

Hydra-NL is organised the same way: 'libsrc\\Bibliotheek\\' holds the routines that every water system uses
('Stapgrootte.f90', 'Hydra_contour.f90', 'interpolatiefuncties.f90', 'verwerkgolf.f90'), next to the families per
area ('*_M'/'*_R' for the lakes and upper rivers, '*_VIJ' for the IJssel-Vecht delta, '*_B' for the lower rivers).
This module is that library, plus the breakdown and percentile output of 'percentielen_Zoet.f90' that Hydra-NL also
shares over all its fresh water systems. Code that differs per water system (which stochastic is slow, how the block
probability is determined, which barrier there is and when it closes) does not belong here.

### Two interpolators

'inextrp1d_interp' and 'inextrp1d_fractions' calculate the same linear inter- and extrapolation, but not with the
same floating point operations: the first builds on 'np.interp' plus a slope beyond the edges, the second on Hydra's
own pattern of a lower index with a fraction ('INITIALISEER_INTERPOLATIE' and 'INEXTRP1D_INIT', with 'I_ONDER' and
'FRACS'). On random grids they differ up to about 1e-12. That is negligible in every result, but not zero, and
comparisons with Hydra-NL are made bit for bit. Merging them would shift numbers without improving anything, so both
are kept, each with a name that says which implementation it is. The same holds for the two variants of
'probability_density'.

### Two ports of CONTOUREN_SAMENVOEGEN

'merge_along_axis' is the simple variant (sort on the second axis, thin out three or more equal values) and
'merge_contours' the full port of 'contourbewerking.f90'. They do not give the same result everywhere, so both are
kept.

## hydra/compiled_contour.py

Compiled counterpart of 'Contour.isoline_python' (ISOLIJN, marching squares). numba is optional: without it, the
caller uses the Python route, with the same results.

The results are bit for bit equal to the Python route. Therefore:

* 'fastmath' is off (the numba default), so that nothing is reordered;
* the operations are in exactly the same order as in 'library', including the sum '0 + z0 + z1 + z2 + z3' that
  Python's 'sum()' over a generator does;
* the points follow the same loop order: bottom, right, top, left, then the closed contours.

The Python route grows its output with 'list.append'; here the buffer is allocated beforehand. If it fills up, no
result is made up: 'isoline_kernel' returns -1 and 'isoline' returns None, so that the caller uses the Python
route.

## hydra/compiled_interpolation.py

Compiled counterpart of 'HydraInterpolate.inextrp1d_fractions' (INEXTRP1D). numba is optional: without it, the caller
uses the numpy route, with the same results.

The results are bit for bit equal to the numpy route. The operation is purely elementwise, so per point the same
sequence of operations is carried out:

```
j  = clip(searchsorted(xp, x) - 1, 0, len(xp) - 2)
fr = (x - xp[j]) / (xp[j+1] - xp[j])
y  = fp[j] * (1 - fr) + fp[j+1] * fr
```

Two edge cases where numpy differs from a naive binary search:

* 'np.searchsorted' with side='left' is 'bisect_left', which is copied literally in the kernel.
* numpy places a NaN in 'x' at the end (i = len(xp)), whereas a binary search on 'xp[mid] < NaN' (always false)
  ends at 0. That is why the NaN branch is explicit.

## hydra/compiled_lower_river_breakdown.py

The masked contributions of the Rhine-Meuse delta breakdown in one compiled loop.

Per wind direction, barrier state and uncertainty combination: the response table linear to the block grid (first u,
then m, then q), zero where the response does not reach the level (FREQ_UMQKR), and the probability density x du x dm
x weight(q) summed into the marginals over q, m and u. Hydra-NL does the same point by point (FREQDICHTHEID_B).

There are no intermediate arrays on the whole (u, m, q) grid. The response and the mask are bit for bit equal to a
numpy route over the full grid; the sums are not, because the order of summation differs (up to 2e-13 relative).

## hydra/compiled_scans.py

Compiled scans of the illustration points on a 3D loading field with a storm surge barrier (ILLU_PUNTU,
ILLU_PUNTQ and ILLU_PUNTM): per contour point the distance to the origin in the standard normal space, and the
point with the smallest distance.

The contour itself is made with the compiled ISOLIJN ('compiled_contour'); the merging of a contour in several parts
is list work and stays with the caller. The scans start after the contour: one kernel call per iteration.

The results are bit for bit equal to the Python route. That is possible because numba calls scipy's 'ndtri'
directly through its C address in 'scipy.special.cython_special': the same cephes routine that
'scipy.special.ndtri' uses.

'cache=True' is not allowed on the functions that call 'ndtri': its address is baked into the compiled code and can
differ per run, so a cached version would jump to a wrong address. Those functions compile on first use (1-2 s).

NaN values are handled explicitly in 'bracket', 'extremes2', 'extremes4' and 'phi_hydra', because numpy and a
hand written loop differ there without an error: 'np.searchsorted' puts a NaN at the end where a binary search ends
at the start, and 'np.max' over a NaN gives NaN (so '>= 0.99' is false) where 'if v > mx' skips it.

## hydra/compiled_wind_segments.py

The block probability P(H >= h | m, q) as a sum over all wind segments where the loading is above the level, as a
compiled loop.

Hydra-NL reads the block probability as P(U >= u_charac), with u_charac the wind speed where the loading crosses the
level (BLOKKENREKENEN_VIJ). That only holds when the loading rises with the wind, which is why Hydra-NL repairs along
the wind. Here every wind segment with h >= level counts:

```
P(H >= h | m, q) = sum [P(U >= u_begin) - P(U >= u_end)]      (a segment up to the edge of the table: P(U >= u_begin))
```

For a rising table that is one segment from u_charac, so P(U >= u_charac): Hydra-NL's method, without the need for
the wind repair.

The table is first interpolated linearly to the block discharge (INEXTRP1D: lower index clamped, fraction not, so
extrapolating). Whether h is above the level at a wind node follows from h linear along the lake level. Where the
wind crosses follows Hydra-NL's isoline ('crossing'): in every cell of the table a straight piece between the two
edge crossings. Linear in the wind along the block grid line would shift u_charac near the closing wind speed and
with it the barrier share. P(U >= u) is linear on the statistics grid, and 0 beyond UMAX; where the isoline runs
along the edge U = UMAX, Hydra-NL gives P(U >= UMAX), here 0.

## hydra/percentiles.py

The Hydra-NL percentiles of the slow stochastic and the wind speed, for the lakes and the upper rivers.

This is a port of Hydra-NL's breakdown chain (UITSPL and UR): the percentiles of the slow stochastic (the lake level M
or the discharge Q) and of the wind speed, given that a level is exceeded. These are the 'T00x_UITSPL' and 'T00x_UR'
tables in 'uitvoer.html'. The slow stochastic is taken from 'statistics.stochastics_slow' ("a" for the lakes, "q" for
the upper rivers), so that one class covers both water systems.

### One formula for two water systems

Hydra-NL shares the output between the lakes and the upper rivers (PERCENTIELENS, SCHRIJFPERCENTIELEN, PERCENTAGE_UR in
'percentielen_Zoet.f90' and 'uitsplitsingen_VIJ.f90'), but not the breakdown itself: the lakes go through
SPLITSENRD and SPLITSENMQ ('splitsen_VIJ.f90'), the upper rivers through SPLITSEN_B and FREQUENTIE_B ('splitsen_B.f90',
shared with the lower rivers). Both give the same breakdown:

```
contribution(u, s, r) = [density of U for u >= u_characteristic(s, r)] * P(r) * f_S(s) * delta_s
```

This module calculates that formula directly, in the form of SPLITSENMQ, for both systems. Two differences between M
and Q remain, and are flags of '_SlowPeak':

* for the river, BLOKKENREKENEN_R gives the block probability with the wind direction already summed out. That is
  the same as p(s) = sum_r P(r) * P(U >= u_characteristic(s, r) | r), which is calculated here for both;
* OVERSCHRIJDINGSDUUR_Q (formula 4.6) does not clamp the exceedance durations of the wave to at least one block
  duration, OVERSCHRIJDINGSDUUR_M (formula 6.3) does. That is the flag 'clamp_duration'.

The chain for the lakes (Fortran sources in 'progsrc/berekenen_Zoet'):

* PERCENTIELVULLEN and PERCENTIELENS ('percentielen_Zoet.f90'): the seven percentiles (5 to 95 %) from the
  normalised cumulative breakdown, with the half bin convention;
* UITSPLITSEN_FREQ, SPLITSENRD and SPLITSENMQ ('uitsplitsenfreq.f90', 'splitsen_VIJ.f90'): per wind direction r and
  block s the contribution P_pot(U >= u_characteristic(s, r) | r) * f_S(s) * delta_s * P(r). The wind breakdown puts
  that same mass on every u >= u_characteristic, with the density of the potential wind (STAT_WIND, grid
  0:0.2:UMAX);
* BLOKKENREKENEN_M and CONTOURVERWERKING ('blokkenrekenen_M.f90', 'contour.f90'): u_characteristic(s, r) is the wind
  speed at which the isoline load(u, s) = level crosses s, linearly inter- and extrapolated on the block grid and
  clipped to [0, UMAX]. The block probability is p(s) = sum_r P(r) * P_pot(U >= u_characteristic(s, r) | r);
* VERWERKGOLF ('verwerkgolf.f90'): SCHALING per peak, the saturated trapezoid probability divided by the linear
  sum of block probabilities;
* FREQDICHTHM and OVERSCHRIJDINGSDUUR_M ('freqdichtheid_M.f90', formula 6.3 of Geerse 2005.088): the momentary
  frequency density f_S(s) = -d/ds sum_peak delta_peak * f_peak * SCHALING_peak * D(s, peak), with D the number of
  wind blocks that the trapezoid spends above s.

Model uncertainty is the outer loop over the combinations of ONZWAARDEN (water level delta_h, and for the crest level
also the wave factors), weighted with KANSONZ. With ONZ_PAFH = 1 (fully dependent) Hydra-NL accumulates the breakdown
per combination in the same way ('uitsplitsingen_VIJ.f90'). Statistical uncertainty is the choice of the marginal
distributions, see 'Settings.include_statistical_uncertainty'.

The wave shapes are built on Hydra-NL's time axis, see 'WaveProcessing.wave_shapes_on_hydra_axis'.

Only the shape of the breakdown matters: PERCENTIELENS normalises the cumulative distribution, so the absolute scale of
the frequency drops out.

## hydra/illustration_points.py

The Hydra-NL illustration point for the lakes and the upper rivers.

This is a port of Hydra-NL's routine ILLU_PUNTQ ('illustratiepunt_Zoet.f90'). The routine does not depend on the water
system: it branches on REGIO and runs over the slow stochastic, the lake level M (REGIO 1 and 3) or the Rhine discharge
Q (REGIO 2), plus the fast stochastic wind speed U given the wind direction r. The port follows the same
generalisation: the slow stochastic is taken from 'statistics.stochastics_slow' ("a" for the lakes, "q" for the upper
rivers), so that one class covers both water systems. One slow stochastic and one closing situation are covered;
anything else raises a 'NotImplementedError'.

### Method

* the isoline response(u, s) = level, on the loading table per wind direction, refined bilinearly;
* per point the Rosenblatt transformation Y = Phi^-1(F_S(s)), Z = Phi^-1(F_U|r(u)); the wind is independent of the
  slow stochastic, so the conditional probability is the marginal one;
* the illustration point is the point closest to the origin, and beta is that distance.

### Model uncertainty

Hydra-NL has an outer loop IONZ over the uncertainty combinations of ONZWAARDEN ('modelonzekerheden.f90'). Every
combination has the values ONZ(IONZ, 1:4) = [delta_h (added to the water level), f_Hm0, f_Tm-1,0, f_Tp (multiplying
the waves)] and a distance contribution AFSTONZ(IONZ) = eps_h^2 + eps_Hm0^2 + eps_Tm-1,0^2. The total squared distance
is Y^2 + Z^2 + AFSTONZ, and the illustration point is the combination (over IONZ and the isoline) with the smallest
total distance ('uitsplitsingen_VIJ.f90').

The grids of the water level and the wave height come from 'DistributionUncertainty.discretise'. For the waves the
grid is built around 1.0 with sigma and only then multiplied with the bias mu (f = mu * (1 + sigma * eps)).

The correlation only exists between the uncertainty of the wave height and that of the wave period (Hs with Tspec and
Hs with Tp). It enters through the conditional period uncertainty given Hs (MU_TSPEC = 1 + rho * (sigma_ts / sigma_hs) *
(f_hs - 1)); Tp is a deterministic function of the realisation of Tspec and has no dimension of its own in the
distance. That keeps eps_Hm0^2 + eps_Tm-1,0^2 the right Mahalanobis distance. 'discretise' only gives the marginal
grid around 1.0, so the conditionally shifted period grid is built here with the same discretisation.

Statistical uncertainty is the choice of the marginal distributions, see 'Settings.include_statistical_uncertainty'.

## hydra/illustration_points_3d.py

The Hydra-NL illustration point on a 3D loading field with a storm surge barrier: the machinery that every fresh water
system with a barrier shares.

This is a port of the 3D branch of 'illustratiepunt_Zoet.f90'. What differs per water system is in a subclass, one
module per water system ('ijssel_vecht_delta' for the IJssel-Vecht delta).

### Method

* the design point (discharge Q, level M, wind speed U) is the point closest to the origin over the union of three
  families of 2D isolines: ILLU_PUNTQ (fixed discharge, contour in (u, m)), ILLU_PUNTM (fixed level, contour in
  (u, q)) and ILLU_PUNTU (fixed wind speed, contour in (m, q)). There is no 3D optimiser. Every contour comes from
  ISOLIJN, is merged into one polyline by CONTOUREN_SAMENVOEGEN and refined with FACTOR = 10;
* the conditional Rosenblatt transformation runs in the order q, m, u: 'conditional_probabilities' derives F(q|k),
  F(m|q,k) and F(u|m,q,k) from the joint density, normalised per axis with the trapezium rule. The Hydra-NL system
  documentation prescribes that order for all fresh water systems. Which stochastics depend on each other does not
  matter here, that is already in the density that comes in;
* EXTREMEN: where a probability cell jumps from about 0 to about 1 across the barrier ((max - min) >= 0.99), the
  coordinate is set to +MAXINT and the point is excluded;
* the loading table is extended in the wind speed to UMAX (UITBREIDING, linear with the last slope of the table), as
  Hydra-NL does before it calculates the illustration point;
* model uncertainty: the combinations of 'uncertainty_combinations_by_distance', with distance^2 = X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 +
  AFSTONZ and the level shifted per combination (water level: level - delta; wave height: level / f_Hm0; crest
  level: a crest level table per combination).

### The seams

Everything after 'joint_umqk' only consumes the density that comes out of it. Which stochastics depend on each other
and how the barrier works is only in these methods of the subclass:

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| '_level_axis' | the name of the level axis in the loading table |
| 'loading_relevant' | which (r, k) tables are loaded |
| 'check' | whether this water system is accepted |
| 'statistics_grids' | the statistics grids of the level and the discharge |
| 'prepare' | preparation of the water system (densities, barrier tables) |
| 'after_block_grids' | preparation that needs the block grids |
| 'joint_umqk' | the joint density over (u, m, q) per barrier state |
| 'conditional_probabilities_direct' | the Rosenblatt chain directly, instead of from a density |
| 'design_level' | a fixed value of the level in the design point |

The acceptance test for a new water system is conservation: the sum over the barrier states must equal the density
without a barrier. A barrier redistributes probability mass, it does not create it.

This module names no barrier on purpose. The barriers of the water systems work with different tables and different
closing criteria; a fact about one of them belongs in the module of that water system.

The barrier states are indices 0 (open) and 1 (closed) inside this module. Outside it they are the closing situations
k = 1 (open) and k = 2 (closed) of the loading table ('_loading[(r, ik + 1)]'). How 'k' is coded in the statistics
differs per water system; that translation belongs to 'joint_umqk' and therefore to the module of the water system.

## hydra/ijssel_vecht_delta.py

The Hydra-NL illustration point for the IJssel-Vecht delta (REGIO 1): a 3D loading field with the Ramspol barrier.

This is a port of the IJssel-Vecht delta chain of 'illustratiepunt_Zoet.f90'. The 3D machinery (the three contour
families, the Rosenblatt chain q, m, u, the scans, the design point) is in 'illustration_points_3d'; this module only
holds what belongs to the IJssel-Vecht delta.

Joint density of lake level and discharge
------------------------------------------
Lake level and discharge are both slow here, and therefore coupled. Pydra's 'statistics.density_aq' is not used: it
differs from Hydra-NL's DICHTH_MQBLOK (another merging of the joint durations, a running maximum and a normalisation of
the masses), by up to about 7 % in OVKANSMQ, which moves the lake level of the illustration point one bin. The density
is therefore rebuilt with the ported Hydra-NL chain ('joint_density_lake_level_discharge': OVERSCHRIJDINGSDUREN, the
sum of STAT_GEZAMENLIJK and KANSDICHTHEID twice) on pydra's peak density and wave shapes, which equal Hydra-NL's.

### Ramspol barrier

The closing wind speed per (lake level, discharge) comes from the KeringUD data through the ported BLOKSNELHEID. Above
the closing wind speed the probability mass of the wind splits into the failure probability of the barrier (closing
situation 1, open) and one minus that (closing situation 2, closed). At easterly wind directions the barrier never
closes and only the open state exists. Pydra's reader ignores the KeringUD data and uses a fixed split without a wind
dependent closure; this module follows Hydra-NL.

The KeringUD data come from the table 'KeringUD' in the database if it is there. Production databases do not have it;
Hydra-NL then reads the CSV of the region from the folder 'data/ini' of its installation, and so does this module: the
caller passes that folder as 'hydra_ini_directory'.

### Closing situations

Hydra-NL counts IK = 1 as open and IK = 2 as closed; the loading table uses ClosingSituationId 1 (failing barrier,
always open) and 2 (regular closing). Pydra's loading key 'k' follows the database, so the closing situation k of this
module is both: 1 open, 2 closed.

The wind is conditionally independent given the direction, so the density factorises as g(u|r) g(m,q) P(k|u,m,q,r).

## hydra/ijssel_vecht_delta_percentiles.py

The Hydra-NL breakdown, percentiles and frequency line for the IJssel-Vecht delta (REGIO 1), with the split over the
open and closed Ramspol barrier.

This is a port of the breakdown chain of the IJssel-Vecht delta ('progsrc/berekenen_Zoet'), on pydra's intermediate
results:

* BLOKKENREKENEN_VIJ: the block probability P(H >= h | q, m) per (m, q), per wind direction and closing situation,
  mixed over the closing situations as (1 - alpha) * P(functioning) + alpha * P(failing). Instead of one
  characteristic wind speed per cell, the block probability is the sum over the wind segments with h >= level
  ('compiled_wind_segments');
* VERWERKGOLF (REGIO 1): SCHALING(s, k) = GQM / G_SLANG per (lake level peak s, discharge peak k), with the block
  probability evaluated bilinearly on the simultaneous lake level and discharge waves (shared time axis; the shift of
  84 hours is in pydra's lake level wave shape);
* FREQDICHTHQM and OVERSCHRIJDINGSDUREN: the joint frequency density f(m, q), differentiated twice from the sum over
  the trapezia of dm * dq * DICHTH_MQPIEK * SCHALING * DUREN. The durations are those of 'ijssel_vecht_delta';
  pydra's 'density_aq' is not used (see there);
* SPLITSENRD, SPLITSENMQ, BIJDRAGEKERING and BIJDRAGENWIND ('splitsen_VIJ.f90'): the breakdown per wind direction;
* PERCENTIELEN_KERING, PERCENTIELENS ('percentielen_Zoet.f90') and PERCENTAGE_UR, in 'library'.

### Closing situations

On the input side Hydra-NL counts IK = 1 as a functioning barrier (database k = 2, regular closing) and IK = 2 as a
failing barrier (database k = 1, always open). On the output side IK = 1 is open and IK = 2 closed. The physical split
uses the closing wind speed BLOKSNELHEID from the KeringUD data ('ijssel_vecht_delta.BarrierClosingData'); a split on
pydra's k axis would give the failure probabilities (0.01 / 0.99), not open and closed.

### Two loading tables

The breakdown and the frequency line use the loading table as pydra delivers it, with the repairs of the settings,
extended linearly to UMAX and not repaired again: Hydra-NL's repair after the extension makes every level artificially
reachable just below UMAX in the tail. With 'with_repaired_loading' the object also holds Hydra-NL's own table
(repaired, extended to UMAX and repaired again), for comparing the method with Hydra-NL; 'breakdown_of_table' and
'frequency_of_table' calculate on it with 'line=False'.

### Scaling

Hydra-NL's SCHAALUITSPLITS scales every breakdown family to the target frequency. Percentiles and percentages normalise
that absolute scale away, so 'breakdown' leaves it out, as it leaves out NGEGEVENSBLOK (a constant factor). As soon as
an absolute number is taken from the breakdown (the frequency or return period per wind direction or closing
situation) that no longer holds: the density route lies a few percent above the frequency line. Use
'breakdown_scaled' then; see 'Scaling.scale_breakdown'.

Measured gap (times NGEGEVENSBLOK, without model uncertainty, ratio to the frequency line):

```
IJ_1_10-3_dk_00035   2.2 m 1.063 -> 3.8 m 1.061   (flat)
IJ_1_11-1_dk_00147   2.2 m 1.051 -> 3.8 m 1.036   (slightly decreasing)
ZW_1_9-1_dk_00304    1.2 m 1.121 -> 2.8 m 1.017   (clearly decreasing)
```

The gap depends on the level, which is why Hydra-NL scales per level and does not correct with one constant.

### Grids

The breakdown grids of lake level and discharge are pydra's 'ablok' and 'qblok' (equal to Hydra-NL's MBLOK and QBLOK);
the wind speed grid is VECTORVULLEN(0, UMAX, 0.2).

### Model uncertainty

An outer loop over the uncertainty combinations with their probability KANSONZ, the whole chain per combination (fully
dependent, ONZ_PAFH = 100). Water level: level - delta; wave height: level / f_hs; crest level: the crest level table
per combination.

## hydra/rhine_meuse_delta.py

The Hydra-NL illustration point for the Rhine-Meuse delta: a 3D loading field with the Europoort barrier.

The 3D machinery (the three contour families, the Rosenblatt chain q, m, u, the scans, the design point) is in
'illustration_points_3d'; this module only holds what belongs to the Rhine-Meuse delta.

### Factorisation

The sea level and the wind are fast and come from the same storm, so they are dependent; only the discharge is slow.
The joint density is g(u, m, r | q) = P(r) g(m | r) g(u | m, r) given the discharge, which pydra implements in
'StatisticsLowerRiver'. The density is taken from pydra, with the barrier probabilities of 'BarrierEuropoort' already
in it. Three things change on the way in:

* axes: 'calculate_probability' returns (u, q, m); the machinery wants (u, m, q);
* masses: pydra returns the probability mass per cell, the machinery integrates a density with step sizes. The mass
  is divided by the cell volume du dm dq on the statistics grids, with the same step sizes as pydra's bins, so that
  the integral gives the masses back;
* closing situations: the loading table has k = 1 (open) and k = 2 (closed); pydra's statistics code them as 0 and
  11. 'calculate_probability' is asked per closing situation, because the branch that returns both at once
  ('closing_situation=None') fails with a broadcast error on the westerly directions.

### Easterly wind directions

At the nine easterly directions the loading table has no sea level axis (2D in (u, q)) and the barrier never closes.
As in Hydra-NL's ONDKANSEN_ILLU_B, the Rosenblatt chain is then built directly: F(q) the marginal of the discharge,
F(m|q) a constant 0.5 (Phi^-1(0.5) = 0, the sea level adds nothing to beta), F(u|m,q) = 1 - G(u|r), and no mass in the
closed state. The sea level of the design point is the spring tide level of the database (SPRINGTIJ): the unique sea
level over all loading rows with an easterly direction.

## hydra/rhine_meuse_delta_percentiles.py

The Hydra-NL breakdown, percentiles and crest level frequency line for the Rhine-Meuse delta (REGIO 0), with the split
over the open and closed Europoort barrier.

This is a port of the breakdown chain of the lower rivers ('freqdichtheid_B.f90' and 'splitsen_B.f90'), on pydra's
intermediate results:

* FREQDICHTHQ (formula 4.6 [Geerse, 2005.088]): the frequency density of the discharge f_Q(q);
* KANS_UMQKR: the joint density over (u, m, q, k) per wind direction, times f_Q(q);
* FREQ_UMQKR: zero where the loading lies below the level;
* BIJDRAGEN_UMQKR: times du dm dq times KANSONZ;
* FREQ_URK, FREQ_MRK and FREQ_QRK: the marginals, the breakdown families;
* SCHAALUITSPLITS and PERCENTIELEN, in 'library'.

There is no contour, no characteristic wind speed and no evaluation on two simultaneous waves: the Rhine-Meuse delta
integrates directly over the (u, m, q, k) grid, as the quadrature of the failure probability per block in
'illustration_points_3d' does. This module therefore builds on 'HydraRhineMeuseDeltaIllustrationPoint', which holds
the loading tables, the block grids, the density per barrier state and the response tables, and only adds the
breakdown.

### The seam with pydra: one factor in q

KANS_UMQKR builds the bracket P(k|u,m,q,r) f(m|r) f(u|m,r) P(r) first, and multiplies it by the frequency density of
the discharge KANSDQ(q) only at the end. Pydra builds the same bracket, but multiplies it by the probability density
g_q(q) of the discharge. 'HydraRhineMeuseDeltaIllustrationPoint.bracket_umqk' divides g_q out, and this module
multiplies by f_Q(q).

That is allowed because the joint factorises in q when summed over the barrier states: per barrier state the shape
over (u, m) differs over q (the closing probability depends on the discharge), but the sum over k of P(k|.) is 1 and
the other two factors integrate to 1, so that the sum over (u, m, k) of joint * du * dm equals g_q(q) P(r). Measured on
HV_1_20-4_dk_00087: a largest relative deviation of 4.9e-15 to 8.8e-15 over 120 discharges at four wind directions.

### The block probability p(q)

FREQDICHTHQ needs SCHALING(qpeak), which VERWERKGOLF derives from the block probability
p(q) = P(loading >= level | Q = q). Hydra-NL calculates it in BLOKKENREKENEN_B as the sum over the directions and the
barrier states of the masked bracket integrated over (u, m). That is the marginal over (u, m, k) of the same masked
bracket the breakdown comes from; the bracket has no discharge factor, so nothing has to be divided out.

### Two model uncertainties, one per barrier state

The HRD table 'UncertaintyModelFactor' has a column 'ClosingSituationId'; on DK_1_22-1_dk_00291 sigma is 0.25 m for an
open and 0.30 m for a closed barrier. Hydra-NL calculates with both ('WS_PAR_PER_KERING' is always on for REGIO 0) and
shifts the water level per barrier state with its own delta. The probabilities stay one vector: the bin edges lie in
standard normal units, so the lists per barrier state have the same weights in the same order, and Hydra-NL walks them
in lockstep with one KANSONZ per combination. The constructor refuses lists with different weights.

### Grids

The discharge and the sea level are the block grids of the illustration point. The wind speed is the block grid on
which pydra delivers the density (about 0.55 m/s); Hydra-NL calculates with USTAP = 0.5 for REGIO 0. Hydra-NL prints
its UITSPL tables on a coarser grid from 'invoer.hyd' (UITQSTAP, UITMSTAP, UITWSTAP); that does not matter for
percentiles, which are values of the stochastic and not bin contents.

### Scaling

NGEGEVENSBLOK is left out of the breakdown: a constant factor that drops out of percentiles and percentages. As soon as
an absolute number is taken from the breakdown, use 'breakdown_scaled'; see 'Scaling.scale_breakdown'.

### Crest level frequency line

'crest_level_line' is the frequency line of the crest level with the crest level per situation in the loading table.
In the Rhine-Meuse delta one water level per barrier state, discharge and sea level comes with different waves, so a
crest level as a function of (water level, u, r) is not enough. Every point (q, m, k, u, r) gets its crest level from
its own waves, and the line follows pydra's water level line: refine to the statistics grid, repair, and sum the
probabilities per level class over the slow stochastic. The refinement is a matrix built after
'LoadingModel.refine', applied to every crest level table; 'check_refine_source' refuses when 'refine' changes.

## hydra/coast_breakdown.py

The Hydra-NL breakdown and percentiles for the coast.

This is a port of BEREKEN_FAALKANSZEE ('watersysteem_zee.f90'), the salt branch of Hydra-NL for REGIO 5: the Wadden
Sea, the Holland coast and the Western Scheldt. The Eastern Scheldt (REGIO 4) is not covered: there Hydra-NL selects
ten illustration points with HOOGSTE_BIJDRAGEN instead of filling every direction. Pydra gives exactly those REGIO 5
locations the class 'StatisticsCoast', and that is the check at the start.

The coast has no slow stochastic: sea level and wind speed are both fast within the same block. The machinery of
'percentiles.py' (peaks, block grids, wave shapes, exceedance durations) therefore does not exist here.

### Method

Per wind direction:

1. ISOLIJN on the loading field B(u, m) at the requested level gives the contour (WU, WM), on the grid of the
  loading table;
2. if the contour contains the sentinel, CONTOUREN_SAMENVOEGEN;
3. if the contour is vertical (min(WM) equals max(WM)), ZUIVER_ZEEWS and KANSEN_ZUIVER_ZEE: the probability is read
  from the exceedance curve of the sea level at the contour level;
4. otherwise VERFIJNEN_CONTOUR gives the characteristic wind speed per sea level, and KANSEN_CONTOURZEE sums the
  cells with a hard indicator on the grid nodes: a cell counts as soon as USTAT(IU) >= UKARAK(IM).

For a water level calculation the local water level at the coast is exactly the sea level, the isoline is always
vertical and Hydra-NL takes route 3, in which the step size of the sea level drops out. For the crest level the loading
depends on the wind, the isoline is slanted and route 4 applies. Route 4 depends on 'settings.m_step'; the caller sets
it as Hydra-NL calculates (MSTAP), this module uses it as it comes in.

### Repair

The loading field is repaired with REPAREER_ZOUT: a falling cell is set equal to its neighbour. Pydra's own
'LoadingModel.repair' makes it strictly larger by 1e-6 per step instead, which tilts an exactly vertical isoline and
thereby the choice between route 3 and route 4. The vertical test therefore allows exactly that artificial slope.

### Model uncertainty

As in Hydra-NL the outer loop is over the uncertainty combinations ('rekenen_onzekerheden.f90'): per combination the
whole loading chain again, and the breakdowns summed with the weight KANSONZ. The coastal databases have no water level
uncertainty, so a water level calculation has a single combination. For the wave height and the wave period Hydra-NL
applies the model uncertainty to the level instead of to the loading field; that route is not covered.

## hydra/coast_illustration_points.py

The Hydra-NL illustration points for the coast.

This is a port of ILLU_PUNT_BEPALEN and ONDKANSEN_ILLU ('illustratiepunt_Zout.f90'). Per wind direction the design
point is the point on the contour with the smallest distance to the origin in standard normal space. The coast covers
the same locations as 'coast_breakdown' (REGIO 5).

### Method

* The loading field is put on the grid of the statistics, not on that of the loading table: for the sea Hydra-NL
  sets WATERSTANDEN%U = STATISTIEK%USTAT and WATERSTANDEN%M = STATISTIEK%MSTAT ('watersysteem_zee.f90'). The waves
  are interpolated to that grid first, and the crest level is calculated per cell afterwards; the other way round
  (interpolating the crest level of the coarse grid) gives a different contour.
* The field is repaired with REPAREER_ZOUT and the isoline is taken at the level.
* Every segment of the contour is divided linearly into ten pieces; the last segment gets one point more, so that
  its end point is included.
* The distance is bivariate: X^2 + Y^2, with X from the sea level and Y from the wind speed given that sea level.
  The wind direction is the outer loop and adds nothing to the distance within a direction (Rosenblatt).
* The non-exceedance probabilities come from the cell probabilities KANS_MUR of the statistics, as cumulative sums
  of half cell masses: ONDKANSM over the sea level and ONDKANSUDM over the wind given the sea level.

Every wind direction gets an illustration point ('uitsplitsingen_Zout.f90' calls ILLU_PUNT_VULLEN for all directions).
The single main illustration point of HOOFDIP4OVERZICHT ('IPuitvoer_Zout.f90') is the direction with the largest
contribution to the exceedance frequency, not the one with the smallest distance; on equal contributions the lowest
direction index wins.

### Model uncertainty

The outer loop is over the uncertainty combinations, and per direction the point with the smallest total distance
X^2 + Y^2 + AFSTONZ stays ('uitsplitsingen_Zout.f90'); on equal distances the first combination wins. A direction can
therefore choose a different combination than its neighbour.

### Influence factors

Hydra-NL prints no influence factors. 'alpha2' is the standard FORM decomposition alpha^2_i = u_i^2 / beta^2 of the
Rosenblatt coordinates, with the same function as the lakes and upper rivers. The term of the water level uncertainty
is left out: the coastal databases have none, and a bar of zero would suggest a measured negligible influence.
